segments.title: Introduction to the lab
segments.text: [[home]] [[lab:preset:mf-1100]] An imagined June morning in the south of Sweden, more than half a century ago: a tractor is setting out for the fields. It runs on wood, with a thread of diesel. [[frame:chip-barn]] One wood chip is stored dry in the barn, with thousands of others. [[frame:drum-chipper]] It was cut by the knives of a chipper. [[scene:tractor]] The tractor carries it off to the field. [[frame:roof-rack]] It rides on the roof rack, before dropping into the bunker. [[scene:gasifier]] The chip sinks gently, in about an hour. [[lab:journey:0.15]] It dries. [[lab:journey:0.42]] Then it blackens and falls apart. [[lab:journey:0.62]] It passes under a flame: a fire short of air, on purpose. [[lab:journey:0.85]] In a bed of red-hot charcoal, the gas cools and becomes fuel. [[lab:journey:0.98]] At the bottom, almost nothing is left. [[scene:gas-train]] The gas carries on, still very hot: [[frame:filter-box]] it crosses a filter, then a cooler. [[frame:cylinder-cutaway]] In the cylinder, that thread of diesel lights it. A Swedish institute tested this tractor on a bench, and a report tells of it. Forty kilowatts at the shaft: eighteen per cent of the energy that went in. So, by our sum, about two hundred and twenty kilowatts going in. [[scene:garage]] By evening, in the garage, the engine stops. [[lab:scenario:engine-stops]] [[frame:post-gas-plume]] The gas does not stop with it: the last world is about that moment. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]] [[scene:farm]] First, a few pointers. There are five worlds, from the farm to the garage. Click a part: its sheet opens, and you can listen to its story. [[mode:assembly]] Assembly tells, in the past tense and without any procedure, how the system may have gone together, in our reading. [[mode:install]] Installation says what had to be gathered before the first day. [[mode:sim]] The simulation lets you change the load and the moisture of the wood. [[mode:lessons]] Seven lessons explain the physics. [[mode:plans]] Ten drawings sketch it. [[mode:explore]] One last thing: this laboratory is an independent educational reconstruction. It is neither an official design nor a maker’s product. It explains a machine from history, and gives no plans. The published figures come from that report, a Swedish book on gasifiers, and some handbooks. The others come out of the simulation. On the sheets, a figure with no mark is published; a cross marks a calculation, a star an estimate. The Sources panel says who said what. [[select:none]]

segments.title: The farm and its wood
segments.text: [[home]] A large farm in the south of Sweden, around nineteen seventy. [[flows:on]] [[frame:chip-barn]] The wood begins here, in the dry of the barn. [[frame:drum-chipper]] The chipper cuts it into small chips, [[frame:chip-sieve]] and the sieve rids them of their fines. [[frame:wood-gas-tractor]] The tractor carries them off, and drags [[frame:clod-crusher]] a four-metre clod crusher behind it. [[frame:ash-bin]] What the machine leaves behind, the ash, [[frame:condensate-barrel]] and some black water, ends up in a bin and in a barrel. [[flows:off]] [[frame:farm-garage]] And there, built against the house, the garage. We will come back to it. [[home]] The farm has no source. Its walls are drawn to the scale of a five-tonne tractor. What is real is what the machine did there: more than two thousand five hundred hours in six years.

segments.title: The tractor and its system
segments.text: [[home]] On paper, the machine rolls on the spot. [[frame:tractor-chassis]] An ordinary tractor, and on its left flank, [[frame:gasifier-unit]] the gasifier: four hundred and fifty kilos more. [[frame:cab]] Its top almost reaches the driver’s eye. [[xray:on]] The cab fades away. [[xray:off]] [[frame:roof-rack]] On the roof, a rack carries the day’s chips. [[frame:gas-line-run]] [[flows:on]] And the gas runs to the engine, through a filter and a cooler. [[flows:off]] [[home]] [[explode:0.6]] Pulled apart, the parts show what carries what. [[explode:0]]

segments.title: The journey of a wood chip
segments.text: [[home]] [[lab:preset:mf-1100]] In this world the apparatus is always shown in section, with its chip. [[frame:spring-lid]] It goes in through the lid, and there, [[frame:chip-column]] [[lab:journey:0.05]] the column draws it gently downwards, in about an hour. [[frame:drying-zone]] [[lab:journey:0.15]] First it dries, and the water vapour escapes. [[frame:pyrolysis-zone]] [[lab:journey:0.42]] Then it breaks down into charcoal and vapours. [[frame:oxidation-zone]] [[lab:journey:0.62]] Those vapours must cross the flame. [[frame:reduction-zone]] [[lab:journey:0.85]] After that the hot gas crosses red-hot charcoal, where it cools: that is where it becomes fuel. [[frame:ash-pit]] [[lab:journey:0.98]] A little ash is left, at the end of the journey. [[lab:journey:0.62]] [[home]] The journey cursor and the gasifier’s drawings are not to scale: on purpose. The section is drawn to scale. [[flows:on]] Air goes in, gas comes out. [[flows:off]]

segments.title: The gas line
segments.text: [[home]] [[lab:preset:mf-1100]] Here the parts stand in the order the gas passes them, from the outlet to the engine. [[flows:on]] [[frame:hot-gas-pipe]] It leaves hot, and the pipe keeps it hot: cooled too soon, it would wet the filter. [[frame:filter-box]] Here, a cloth catches the fine dust. [[frame:gas-cooler]] Then the cooler drops it to about twenty degrees, in the model, because colder gas is denser. [[frame:gas-air-mixer]] At the mixer, it meets fresh air again. [[frame:cylinder-cutaway]] In the cylinder, a thread of diesel lights it. [[flows:off]] [[home]] On the floor, ribbons show where the energy goes. The wood going in, the gas, the diesel, the work at the shaft, and in grey, the losses. The grey far outweighs the work.

segments.title: What it does when you stop
segments.text: [[home]] [[lab:scenario:closed-garage]] Back in the garage, the same tractor is parked under a bedroom. [[frame:post-gas-plume]] The engine is off. But the gas keeps forming in the fuel, still hot, and it comes out, even from a machine that looked tight. [[flows:on]] [[lab:speed:600]] [[frame:co-indicator]] The indicator has a lamp, which lights as soon as carbon monoxide has touched the room and stays lit. [[frame:room-above]] Upstairs, the bedroom gets some in its turn, later. [[flows:off]] [[frame:garage-door]] At start-up, a fan draws air through the apparatus; it gives off carbon monoxide, and so does the engine at idle. The Swedes found it far from satisfactory to start either with the garage doors open. Here the engine is off. [[lab:door:open]] In the model, with the door open, the room’s carbon monoxide falls fast. That is what a well-mixed box gives, by construction. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]] [[home]] As for how long the gas keeps coming out like this, the sources disagree.

segments.title: Wood-gas tractor
segments.text: This five-tonne tractor runs on wood, with a thread of diesel. At forty kilowatts at the shaft, the model burns thirty-four kilos of chips an hour. The Swedish institute’s bench measured forty-one. The gap comes from the model: its engine burns better than the bench’s, and so does its gasifier. The regular drivers would not have it, because the work was time-consuming, dirty and heavy.

segments.title: Chip barn
segments.text: One eight-hour shift devours more than a cubic metre of chips. Moisture matters as much as quantity: the report on the institute gives thirty per cent moisture as the limit. And wood pellets kept in a closed store give off carbon monoxide by themselves.

segments.title: Drum chipper
segments.text: A wood-gas tractor does not burn logs. The chips are made here, in a drum fitted with knives that cuts the wood into pieces. Size matters, because the gas has to pass between them. By the report on the institute, suitable chips mostly measure fifteen to thirty millimetres.

segments.title: Chip sieve
segments.text: Fines are the splinters and the dust, which block the gas’s way. On a tractor of the same family, sieved chips gave a quarter more power. The cost: fourteen per cent of the wood thrown away. The model finds only ten per cent gain here, since it counts nothing but the pressure drop.

segments.title: Clod crusher
segments.text: A clod crusher four metres wide, dragged behind the tractor, is what the whole machine exists for. More than two thousand five hundred hours of service in six years, haulage included. On screen, it stands still.

segments.title: Farmhouse
segments.text: No source we read describes the farmhouse: this one is an estimate, two storeys of red boards. The Swedish book on gasifiers ranks among the worst accidents those of cars with a leaking lid. Parked under a room where people live. So the garage touches the house.

segments.title: Farm garage
segments.text: Why a garage, in a lab about wood? In Sweden, two thousand eight hundred and sixty-five vehicles, most of them gasifier vehicles, caught fire in five years. Often from an electrical fault, says the Swedish book on gasifiers. Many garage fires, often at night, had no known cause. In the first quarter of nineteen forty-two alone: nearly four a day.

segments.title: Ash bin
segments.text: The gasifier does not leave only gas. It leaves ash, and charcoal that never finished its journey: up to three point five per cent of the fuel. And that ash is hot: an American source lists hot ash among the fire risks.

segments.title: Condensate barrel
segments.text: Black water ends up here. As it cools, the gas leaves water loaded with tars. Typically, it holds one thousand five hundred to three thousand milligrams of phenols per litre. That is one hundred and fifty to three hundred times wartime Sweden’s sewer limit. For its fate, ask your local authority.

segments.title: Field ditch
segments.text: A ditch runs beside almost every lowland farm. This one does nothing, on purpose, and nothing flows in it. One question remains: where did the black water go? On the two large farms where this tractor worked, nothing we have read says.

segments.title: Tractor chassis
segments.text: Without its gasifier, this is an ordinary tractor. The system weighs four hundred and fifty kilos: nearly nine per cent of the gas version’s mass. [[explode:0.7]] Everything else leaves the chassis, each along its own line. [[explode:0]] The Swedish institute also removed the front weights, and turned the air filter round.

segments.title: Cab
segments.text: Where you drive. The top of the gasifier comes right under the driver’s eye: three to eighteen centimetres of margin. [[xray:on]] The cab fades away, and the top of the gasifier reads right against the eye. [[xray:off]] Nothing we have read measures the air in the cab.

segments.title: Roof rack
segments.text: Only forty to fifty minutes of chips fit in the bunker. The rest rides on the roof, above the driver: one eight-hour shift takes more than two hundred kilos. The report on the institute does not say whether it was a good choice; it was, at any rate, necessary.

segments.title: Roof headlights
segments.text: A tiny part, to say that a tractor really gets modified. The Swedish institute moved the headlights to the roof. According to the report on the institute, the left one would have been hidden by the gasifier.

segments.title: Rear wheels
segments.text: Big wheels, to push the machine and its weight: tyres forty-seven centimetres wide. On screen they make one turn about every three seconds, an estimate. Slow enough that the eye never sees them turn backwards.

segments.title: Front wheels
segments.text: [[lab:scenario:engine-stops]] When the engine stops, the wheels stop rolling. They are smaller than the rear wheels. They are also lightened: the Swedish institute removed the front weights to make room for the cooler. How the steering took it, no source we read says. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Diesel engine
segments.text: On diesel alone, this six-cylinder gives sixty-four kilowatts; on gas with a thread of diesel, fifty-one. The gas and air mixture holds less energy than a petrol mixture. Two thousand five hundred kilojoules per cubic metre, against three thousand eight hundred. The model finds fifty-five kilowatts, close to the bench’s fifty-one. That agreement is worth little: it reads thirty per cent too high on the other engines.

segments.title: Injection pump
segments.text: Even on gas, the diesel keeps its pump, which doses the thread of diesel the flame needs. But it sits under the bonnet, right beside the gasifier. At twenty-five hours, it seized, for want of cooling and lubrication, says the report on the institute. The institute then added a radiation shield, against the gasifier’s heat.

segments.title: Heat shield
segments.text: This shield was added after the injection pump seized: it is the trace of it. The gasifier’s casing reaches about two hundred and ten degrees, an estimate. Neither the material nor the size of the shield is given.

segments.title: Extra governor
segments.text: A diesel holds its speed with a governor that acts on the fuel. Here most of the energy comes from the gas: our reading is that a second governor was needed, on the gas throttle. A belt links it to the fan’s shaft.

segments.title: Left consoles
segments.text: Four hundred and fifty kilos on one flank: that is an imbalance. The report on the institute does not say how it dealt with it. Bolted consoles carry the gasifier, fifty centimetres off the ground.

segments.title: Gasifier unit
segments.text: The top of the gasifier is two metres twenty-two above the ground. Chips go down into it, and gas comes out. [[xray:on]] The fire glows through the lower casing. [[xray:off]] On the bench, the gas is worth five point six megajoules per cubic metre; the model finds five point three.

segments.title: Gas line run
segments.text: The gas does not go straight from the gasifier to the engine: a hot pipe, a valve, a filter, a cooler, a mixer. [[flows:on]] The dots follow it, and change colour as it cools. [[flows:off]] All along, the engine sucks: about seventy-two millibars of loss at most, an estimate.

segments.title: Spring lid
segments.text: A lid and a spring. If the lid does not close, air comes in at the top. The Swedish book on gasifiers says a parked one may then start burning like a stove. The model tries three leaks: the biggest lasts about six hours, while there is wood.

segments.title: Fuel casing
segments.text: The bunker: the top of the gasifier, two hundred litres of chips, about thirty kilos. At full load it empties in forty to fifty minutes: that is the rhythm of the day. And two researchers died of carbon monoxide after climbing down into a gasifier’s bunker.

segments.title: Chip column
segments.text: [[lab:journey:0.05]] This machine has two speeds. By our sum, the column sinks about a centimetre and a half a minute, and a chip takes an hour to come down. The gas crosses the same bed in a few hundredths of a second. Wood moves at a snail’s pace, gas in one breath. [[lab:journey:0.62]]

segments.title: Drying zone
segments.text: [[lab:journey:0.15]] At the top of the column, the fire’s heat drives the water out of the wood: it leaves as steam. Beyond about forty per cent moisture, the report on the institute says, the gas no longer burns. [[lab:moisture:40]] At forty per cent, the model burns fifty-seven kilos an hour, instead of thirty-four. Its flame never goes out: what stops a real hearth is not in it. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Pyrolysis zone
segments.text: Lower down, the wood turns into something else. From about two hundred and fifty degrees, it breaks down [[lab:journey:0.42]] into charcoal, and vapours of gas and tar. They are the gasifier’s real problem: left alone, tars stick to everything. They still have to cross the flame. [[lab:journey:0.62]]

segments.title: Oxidation zone
segments.text: The fire. [[lab:journey:0.62]] One thousand two hundred to one thousand five hundred degrees, in general, the report on the institute says. The model finds one thousand two hundred and thirty-five, and one thousand and seventy-six with the wall’s loss. The vapours must cross this flame. Almost no tar comes out: about zero point zero three per cent of the wood, on the bench. An updraught gasifier leaves five to twenty per cent. A fire short of air makes gas; a fire with enough air leaves only ashes.

segments.title: Reduction zone
segments.text: Below the flame, a bed of red-hot charcoal. [[lab:journey:0.85]] The gas cools here, and that is where it becomes fuel. Carbon dioxide takes back carbon and becomes carbon monoxide; steam becomes hydrogen. These reactions take heat, and the gas loses about three hundred and seventy degrees. It leaves, according to the model, with a fifth carbon monoxide, a sixth hydrogen, nearly half nitrogen. [[lab:journey:0.62]]

segments.title: Fuel baffle
segments.text: In the bunker, the fuel stuck to the wall, in the pyrolysis zone, where tars condense. It formed bridges. The report on the institute says a baffle that removes this contact brought the problem down to what was judged acceptable.

segments.title: Condensate sleeve
segments.text: Instead of letting the wood’s water run down and cool the fire, we make it condense elsewhere. [[flows:on]] The steam crosses the perforations, touches the cold wall, and runs down to the drain. [[flows:off]] Sixty to eighty per cent of the wood’s water can be drained off this way.

segments.title: Condensate drain
segments.text: Out of this drain goes the black water, to a bin. Without the bin, the report on the institute says, it would come back and wet the charcoal bed after a stop. The model counts one point nine litres an hour at eight per cent moisture, five point seven at twenty.

segments.title: Eccentric lock
segments.text: Two bodies make up the gasifier, the top holding the fuel and the bottom holding the fire. [[explode:0.5]] A band holds them together, and this lock tightens the band. [[explode:0]] [[lab:scenario:air-leak]] But every joint lets air in, and that air burns the finished gas, near the grate. The gas falls from five point three to four point two megajoules per cubic metre. The size of the leak is a guess; the direction is not: the gas comes out hotter and weaker. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Outer casing
segments.text: At full load, the gasifier’s hot outer skin reaches about two hundred and ten degrees, in the model. [[xray:on]] The upper body fades, and the fire glows through the lower casing. [[xray:off]] Two accounts of its losses do not agree: both are kept.

segments.title: Air intake
segments.text: Here comes the fire’s air, drawn in by the engine: the whole line is under suction. When the engine stops, the suction ends, and the gas keeps forming. The direction reverses: white or yellow gas has been seen coming out here.

segments.title: Air nozzles
segments.text: Air for the fire comes in through the nozzles, in a ring around the fire box. No pressure pushes it: the engine draws it in. [[flows:on]] It goes round, then shares out. [[flows:off]] Too much air, and all the wood would burn: no gas. No air, no flame.

segments.title: Fire box
segments.text: The pot that holds the fire. The air passes between it and the casing before entering the fire. It is one of the parts that wear fastest. It cracks between six hundred and a thousand hours, on the record of several vehicles. The report on the institute gives the life of some critical parts.

segments.title: Throat ring
segments.text: All the fire’s gas must pass through this constriction, at the hottest point. Vapours and tars come down with the wood. If they skirted the flame, they would come out as they are. The ring forces them through it. It lasts about seven hundred hours, says the report on the institute, then is replaced. Here we say what this part does, and nothing of how it is made.

segments.title: Grate
segments.text: Under the charcoal bed, the grate carries the charcoal, and lets ash and gas through. And it moves: according to the report on the institute, chips clogged a fixed grate in under an hour. The programme’s grates lasted four hundred to seven hundred hours.

segments.title: Grate linkage
segments.text: The grate is in the fire, and the crank outside: a shaft crosses the wall, on the gas side. So the grate is worked from outside, without opening the body. On screen, crank and grate turn on one axis, joined by the shaft.

segments.title: Ash pit
segments.text: The hollow under the grate receives what has not burned: ash, and charcoal that never finished its journey. [[lab:journey:0.98]] Up to three point five per cent of the fuel. That is worth about five per cent of the power: eight kilowatts in the model, at full load. [[lab:journey:0.62]]

segments.title: Gas outlet
segments.text: Where the gas leaves the gasifier: about two hundred and forty degrees, still hot. [[flows:on]] It goes down through the bed, under the grate, up along the casing, and out here. [[flows:off]] That temperature is an estimate. Hot enough that the gas does not condense in the filter, cool enough that its cloth does not burn.

segments.title: Hot gas pipe
segments.text: The gas enters at about two hundred and forty degrees, and must stay above its dew point. Below it, water and tar condense. The filter cloth gets wet, and its resistance is multiplied by more than six. [[flows:on]] The dots take the colour of the gas’s heat, and lose it as they go. [[flows:off]]

segments.title: Stop valve
segments.text: On the diagram in the report on the institute, a stop valve between the hot pipe and the filter. The report does not say what it was for, and we describe no use of it. Our reading: it changes nothing about what forms in the apparatus.

segments.title: Starting fan
segments.text: When the engine is not yet pulling, a fan takes its place, drawing air through the apparatus. It sends the gas up a stack: about two hundred litres of carbon monoxide a minute, says the Swedish book on gasifiers. Only the trace is kept, with no steps to follow.

segments.title: Fan stack
segments.text: It leaves the hot pipe’s tee, and rises about two and a half metres. It carries the fan’s gas upwards. But a stack does not change the nature of that gas: about a fifth is carbon monoxide, wherever it goes.

segments.title: Primary-air valve
segments.text: On the diagram in the report on the institute, the fire’s air leaves the fan’s eye. It passes this valve, then enters the gasifier. [[flows:on]] The air dots follow that path. [[flows:off]] We give no position and no setting for this valve.

segments.title: Cyclone
segments.text: A good cyclone spins the gas and throws the dust against its walls: sixty to seventy per cent. It appears on the fabric-filter system of the institute’s programme, not on this tractor’s diagram. The report does not say whether it had one, and the photograph cannot settle it.

segments.title: Filter box
segments.text: The box holds the cloth that stops the dust. It was first two and a half square metres, and cleaning it every twenty hours was too much. They doubled it. [[xray:on]] Inside, the bags. [[xray:off]] It is also a place where air can meet gas: a backfire into the filter can be violent.

segments.title: Filter bags
segments.text: The cloth is hung in flat bags: the gas passes through, the dust stays. Behind it, only three tenths of a milligram of dust per cubic metre remains. But the cloth clogs. [[lab:scenario:filter-ageing]] It darkens as dust settles in it. On the truck of the institute’s programme, its resistance doubled around three thousand kilometres. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Gas cooler
segments.text: After the filter, the still-hot gas rises through half the tubes and comes down through the other half. [[flows:on]] The dots turn from red to blue. [[flows:off]] It is cooled because colder gas is denser. By the report on the institute, in general, ten per cent less temperature gives almost two per cent more power. And water comes out: the model counts two point two litres an hour.

segments.title: Condensate vessel
segments.text: The cooler’s black-water vessel. This tractor’s one serious failure probably came from it: overfull, it sent water into the engine. According to the report on the institute, a vessel of this kind was emptied every two to three hours. A simple level to watch, but a dirty, heavy job.

segments.title: Gas-air mixer
segments.text: Here the gas meets the air from the air filter, roughly volume for volume. It takes one point zero eight of air to one of gas, by arithmetic; one point one two in the model. No slider for this proportion: it comes from the gas itself.

segments.title: Gas throttle
segments.text: In an ordinary diesel, the driver’s foot sets the diesel. Here it sets the gas: this throttle says how much comes in. [[lab:scenario:idling]] At idle the lever almost closes, but on the bench fifty-five kilowatts still go in, giving nothing to the shaft. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Secondary-air throttle
segments.text: A second throttle sits on the air added to the gas, the secondary air, as against the fire’s primary air. It sets the proportion. On the truck of the institute’s programme, it was worked by hand, says the report. It is a setting with an optimum, which is not given here.

segments.title: Pilot injector
segments.text: A diesel has no spark plug: it lights its charge by compressing it, then injecting diesel. Gas and air do not light that way, but the thread of diesel does: it is the pilot. So wood is not enough: the pilot stays diesel.

segments.title: Cylinder cutaway
segments.text: Here energy ends up as work: a cylinder cut in two. The real engine turns thirty-one times a second, too fast for the eye. The one on screen turns at six per cent of that. And the gas burns slowly. In general, the report on the institute sees a limit near two thousand five hundred revolutions a minute.

segments.title: Exhaust pipe
segments.text: At the engine’s exit, at work, very little carbon monoxide gets through: three tenths of a per cent in the model. But at idle, the Swedish book on gasifiers read five to eight per cent in the exhaust of wartime engines. The model reads that figure this way: at idle, most of the gas crosses the engine unburnt, two thirds.

segments.title: Water gauge
segments.text: A U-tube full of water: the difference between the two levels gives the filter’s suction. The model reads two hundred and sixteen millimetres of water. [[lab:scenario:filter-ageing]] The gap between the columns grows as the cloth clogs. It says nothing about the gas, only that the filter resists. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Closed garage
segments.text: The room where the machine is parked: fifty cubic metres of air, or a thousand. [[lab:scenario:closed-garage]] [[flows:on]] [[lab:speed:293]] The dots are the carbon monoxide. The model puts one cubic metre of gas in it after the stop. [[lab:pause]] Half an hour later the small room reaches about three thousand five hundred parts per million. The large one, two hundred. But this box is well mixed: a real garage holds this gas in layers, far more concentrated. [[flows:off]] [[lab:play]] [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Garage door
segments.text: The door has three states. [[lab:scenario:closed-garage]] [[lab:speed:421]] Door shut, fifty cubic metres, half an hour after the stop. [[lab:pause]] The model counts about three thousand five hundred parts per million. [[lab:scenario:closed-garage]] [[lab:door:ajar]] [[lab:speed:672]] Door ajar, same half hour. [[lab:pause]] The model counts about two thousand one hundred. The Swedes found it far from satisfactory to run the starting fan or the engine with the garage doors open. Here the engine is not running. [[lab:scenario:closed-garage]] [[lab:door:open]] [[lab:speed:928]] Door open, same half hour. [[lab:pause]] In the model, six hundred and ninety parts per million, far less. [[lab:play]] [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Room above
segments.text: Above the garage, a bedroom with a made bed. The Swedish book on gasifiers says some of the country’s worst accidents came from a car with a leaking lid. Parked under a living space. [[lab:scenario:closed-garage]] [[lab:speed:600]] The gas gets through the floor, at a rate nobody measured. The bedroom climbs to about six hundred and seventy parts per million, more than an hour after the garage’s peak. Nobody is drawn in it. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Post-gas plume
segments.text: The engine stops. [[lab:scenario:engine-stops]] Nothing draws any more, but the gas keeps forming in the fuel, still hot. It pushes for about twenty minutes, says the Swedish book on gasifiers, sometimes for hours according to another manual. It comes out, even from a tight unit, with twenty-three to twenty-seven per cent carbon monoxide. Nobody measured its volume on this machine. The model starts from one cubic metre and lets the push weaken without ever stopping. That choice is the model’s; no measurement gives it. No source we read says when a room holds none of this gas. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Exhaust plume
segments.text: [[lab:preset:mf-1100]] [[lab:place:garage]] An engine can also run in the garage, and its exhaust goes in. At idle, the Swedish book on gasifiers read five to eight per cent carbon monoxide in the exhaust of wartime engines. The grey plume exists only while the engine runs. [[lab:engine:off]] After that, the white of the stop takes over. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: Carbon monoxide indicator
segments.text: On the wall, a dial whose needle follows the model’s carbon monoxide. [[lab:scenario:closed-garage]] [[lab:speed:600]] The lamp lights as soon as carbon monoxide has been in the room. The needle falls back, and the lamp stays lit: a low figure says nothing about a real room. No green zone: the dial shows only the model’s figure. [[lab:preset:mf-1100]]

segments.title: 1940s rescue set
segments.text: On the left, a rescue set from the nineteen forties. The doctors of the day treated the poisoned with methods that are neither described nor recommended here. About ten thousand chronic cases were recorded in Sweden in five years.
